Germany has about 83.5 million people (83,467,117 at the end of 2025), so it is roughly two-thirds the size of Japan, which has about 124 million [1].

The two countries have similar demographics. Both have ageing populations and very low birth rates. Germany recorded 654,241 births in 2025, the lowest since the Second World War, and a fertility rate of 1.32 children per woman [1][2]. Destatis projects that by 2035 one in four Germans will be 67 or older [3].

The main difference is migration. In Germany more people die each year than are born, but immigration has usually made up for it. In 2022, for example, net immigration of about 1.46 million, mostly refugees from Ukraine, raised the population by 1.3% [4]. Japan takes in far fewer immigrants, so its population has been falling steadily since about 2010. The end-of-2025 total is a little below Germany's 2025 average of about 83.6 million, which suggests growth has stalled or dipped slightly. I couldn't confirm the exact change for 2025, though.
